difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE because it links two concepts (ReLU acting as the identity on positive inputs, and forward propagation through a sparse multi-layer network) in a routine three-layer computation, with a connectivity-reading trap, in about 2–3 minutes.
stem:
Consider the two neural networks (NNs) shown in Figures 1 and 2, with $ReLU$ activation ($ReLU(z) = \max\{0, z\}, \forall z \in \mathbb{R}$). $\mathbb{R}$ denotes the set of real numbers. The connections and their corresponding weights are shown in the Figures. The biases at every neuron are set to 0. For what values of $p, q, r$ in Figure 2 are the two NNs equivalent, when $x_1, x_2, x_3$ are positive?

**Figure 1**

![Figure: Figure 1, a feed-forward network. Inputs x1, x2 and x3 feed a layer of three neurons: x1 connects to all three, x2 to the top and bottom neurons, and x3 to the middle and bottom neurons, each with weight 1. Each of these three neurons connects to both neurons of the next layer with weight 2. Those two neurons connect to a single output neuron with weights 3 and 3.](/pyq/2024/fig/Q43-1.png)

**Figure 2**

![Figure: Figure 2, a single-layer network. Inputs x1, x2 and x3 connect directly to one output neuron with weights p, q and r respectively.](/pyq/2024/fig/Q43-2.png)

solution.quick: All weights are positive, the biases are 0 and the inputs are positive, so every pre-activation is positive and each $ReLU$ acts as the identity. Figure 1 therefore collapses to a linear map. Each input-to-output path has weight $1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 = 6$. $x_1$ has $3 \times 2 = 6$ paths and $x_2$, $x_3$ each have $2 \times 2 = 4$, so the output is $36x_1 + 24x_2 + 24x_3$. Hence $p = 36$, $q = 24$, $r = 24$, which is option **(A)**.

steps.title: Read the connections in Figure 1
steps.body:
Label the first hidden layer $h_1, h_2, h_3$ (top to bottom), the second hidden layer $u_1, u_2$, and the output $y$. The first layer is **not** fully connected: it has 7 edges, not 9.

| Neuron | Incoming edges (weight) |
| --- | --- |
| $h_1$ (top) | $x_1$ (1), $x_2$ (1) |
| $h_2$ (middle) | $x_1$ (1), $x_3$ (1) |
| $h_3$ (bottom) | $x_1$ (1), $x_2$ (1), $x_3$ (1) |
| $u_1$ | $h_1, h_2, h_3$ (2 each) |
| $u_2$ | $h_1, h_2, h_3$ (2 each) |
| $y$ | $u_1$ (3), $u_2$ (3) |

So $x_1$ feeds all three first-layer neurons, $x_2$ feeds only $h_1$ and $h_3$, and $x_3$ feeds only $h_2$ and $h_3$.

steps.title: Why ReLU disappears for positive inputs
steps.body: $ReLU(z) = z$ whenever $z \ge 0$. The inputs are positive, every weight is positive and every bias is 0. So each neuron's weighted sum is positive, and its output equals that sum. The same holds layer by layer, so no neuron ever clips to 0. Figure 1 behaves as a purely **linear** network on this domain.

steps.title: Propagate layer by layer
steps.body:
**First hidden layer:**

$$h_1 = x_1 + x_2, \quad h_2 = x_1 + x_3, \quad h_3 = x_1 + x_2 + x_3$$

$$h_1 + h_2 + h_3 = 3x_1 + 2x_2 + 2x_3$$

**Second hidden layer.** Both neurons receive the same inputs with the same weights:

$$u_1 = u_2 = 2(h_1 + h_2 + h_3) = 6x_1 + 4x_2 + 4x_3$$

**Output:**

$$y = 3u_1 + 3u_2 = 6(6x_1 + 4x_2 + 4x_3) = 36x_1 + 24x_2 + 24x_3$$

In matrix form this is $W_3 W_2 W_1 = [3\;\;3]\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = [36\;\;24\;\;24]$.

steps.title: Match with Figure 2
steps.body:
Figure 2 computes $y' = ReLU(p x_1 + q x_2 + r x_3)$. We need $y' = y$ for **every** positive $(x_1, x_2, x_3)$. The left side $y = 36x_1 + 24x_2 + 24x_3$ is positive, so $y'$ must equal the linear expression $p x_1 + q x_2 + r x_3$. Two linear functions that agree on the whole positive orthant have equal coefficients:

$$p = 36, \quad q = 24, \quad r = 24$$

Check at $(x_1, x_2, x_3) = (2, 1, 1)$. Figure 1 gives $h = (3, 3, 4)$, $u_1 = u_2 = 20$ and $y = 120$. Figure 2 with option (A) gives $72 + 24 + 24 = 120$. ✓

solution.teaching:
**What a neuron computes.** A neuron takes a weighted sum of its inputs, adds a bias and applies an activation: $a = \sigma(\sum_i w_i x_i + b)$. For $ReLU$, $\sigma(z) = \max\{0, z\}$. This is piecewise linear: it passes $z$ unchanged when $z \ge 0$ and outputs 0 when $z < 0$.

**When a ReLU network is secretly linear.** The only non-linearity in a ReLU network is the clipping of negative values. If every neuron's pre-activation is guaranteed to be non-negative, nothing is ever clipped, and each layer is just a matrix multiplication. A stack of linear layers is itself linear: $W_3(W_2(W_1 x)) = (W_3 W_2 W_1)x$. That is why a deep network with no active non-linearity has no more expressive power than a single layer. Here, positive inputs, positive weights and zero biases guarantee this.

**Path-sum view.** In a linear network, the coefficient of input $x_i$ in the output equals the sum, over all paths from $x_i$ to the output, of the product of the weights along the path. This is just matrix multiplication written out. It is often the fastest way to collapse a small drawn network.

**Back to this question.** Every path in Figure 1 has the same weight product, $1 \times 2 \times 3 = 6$, so each coefficient is $6 \times (\text{number of paths})$. From $x_1$ there are 3 first-layer targets, each fanning out to 2 second-layer neurons: $3 \times 2 = 6$ paths, giving 36. $x_2$ and $x_3$ each reach only 2 first-layer neurons: $2 \times 2 = 4$ paths, giving 24. Figure 2 is equivalent exactly when $(p, q, r) = (36, 24, 24)$. The whole question turns on counting the first-layer edges correctly.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: It matches the collapsed map $y = 36x_1 + 24x_2 + 24x_3$ of Figure 1, which holds because every $ReLU$ acts as the identity for positive inputs.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: It swaps the roles of $x_1$ and $x_3$. $x_3$ feeds only two first-layer neurons ($h_2$, $h_3$), so its coefficient is $4 \times 6 = 24$. $x_1$ feeds all three, giving 36. At $x_1 = x_2 = x_3$ both A and B give $84x_1$, but at $(2, 1, 1)$ Figure 1 gives 120 while B gives $48 + 24 + 36 = 108$.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: $x_1$ has 6 paths of weight 6, giving 36, not 18. $x_2$ has only 4 paths, giving 24, not 36. At $(1, 1, 1)$, C gives 78 while Figure 1 gives 84.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: $36$ for every input is what a **fully connected** first layer (9 edges) would give. In Figure 1, $x_2$ has no edge to the middle neuron and $x_3$ has no edge to the top neuron, so their coefficients are only 24.

solution.shortcut: Every path has weight $1 \times 2 \times 3 = 6$, so each coefficient is $6 \times (\text{first-layer edges from } x_i) \times 2$. $x_1$ has 3 first-layer edges, giving $6 \times 3 \times 2 = 36$. $x_2$ and $x_3$ have 2 each, giving $6 \times 2 \times 2 = 24$.
solution.commonTrap: Assuming the first layer is fully connected and answering $p = q = r = 36$ (D). Count the edges: $x_2$ skips the middle neuron and $x_3$ skips the top one. Also, testing only with $x_1 = x_2 = x_3$ cannot separate (A) from (B), because both give $84x_1$. Use unequal test values.

transcription.notes: Transcribed from the official paper rendering and independently checked against it. Figures 1 and 2 are the raster images embedded in the official PDF, copied unchanged as Q43-1.png (Figure 1, the multi-layer network) and Q43-2.png (Figure 2, weights p, q, r); both were viewed and confirmed to match the crop. They carry faint traces of the 'GATE 2024' watermark. The Figure 1 connectivity was re-read by the verifier from an enlarged rendering: 7 input-to-hidden edges, all weight 1 (x1 to all three neurons, x2 to top and bottom, x3 to middle and bottom); 6 hidden-to-second-layer edges, all weight 2; and 2 output edges of weight 3. The paper typesets the options with uneven spacing (e.g. 'p = 36, q = 24,r = 24'); spacing is normalised in LaTeX without changing values.

answerVerification.checkCode:
import numpy as np
relu=lambda z: np.maximum(0,z)
# Figure 1 edges read from the figure (all input->hidden weights 1):
# h1<-x1,x2 ; h2<-x1,x3 ; h3<-x1,x2,x3
W1=np.array([[1,1,0],[1,0,1],[1,1,1]])
W2=2*np.ones((2,3))          # every hidden neuron -> both 2nd-layer neurons, weight 2
W3=np.array([[3,3]])         # both -> output, weight 3
net1=lambda x: relu(W3@relu(W2@relu(W1@x)))
print('linear map for x>0:', W3@W2@W1)   # [[36 24 24]]
opts={'A':(36,24,24),'B':(24,24,36),'C':(18,36,24),'D':(36,36,36)}
rng=np.random.default_rng(0); X=rng.uniform(0.01,10,(3,1000))
for k,(p,q,r) in opts.items():
    net2=relu(np.array([[p,q,r]])@X)
    print(k, np.allclose(net1(X),net2))
answerVerification.notes: Verifier solved blind before seeing the key, after re-reading the Figure 1 edges from an enlarged crop: with positive inputs, positive weights and zero biases every ReLU acts as the identity, so h1 = x1+x2, h2 = x1+x3, h3 = x1+x2+x3, both second-layer neurons equal 2(3x1+2x2+2x3), and the output is 36x1+24x2+24x3, giving (p, q, r) = (36, 24, 24), option (A). Composing the weight matrices gives W3·W2·W1 = [36, 24, 24], and a numpy check on 1000 random positive inputs shows only option A reproduces the Figure 1 output. This matches the official key A.
